introduction: “Consort with the followers of all religions in a spirit of friendliness and fellowship.” Bahá’u’lláh repeats the sentence in tablet after tablet, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá spends a lifetime applying it: to strangers, to neighbouring farms, to other people’s churches and mosques, to enemies, to tedious visitors. A hundred of the guide’s 189 quotations are given here, ten from each tenth of its length, including the talks in which ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says where the command stops. Beside them stand a hundred voices from elsewhere: the law of the stranger in Leviticus, the Sermon on the Mount, the Qur’an on churches and mosques, Ashoka’s rock edict, Ibn ‘Arabí, Mozi and his critic Mencius, Aristotle on how many friends a person can have, Frost’s wall. Most stand close to the reading they follow. About one in six doubts that love can be universal, or draws the line somewhere else, and those end in a question.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks for kindness “never asking whether they deserve to be loved”. Dostoevsky’s doctor loves humanity and cannot bear his neighbour. Which is harder for you, and what helps?

“Call none a stranger … Be ye as if all men were your close kin.” Mencius thought that loving all equally wrongs one’s own family, and Aristotle that perfect friendship is for few. How do the readings answer them?
The glad tidings is that association with all religions is permitted. Read Ezra, the woman at the well and Peter’s vision. What were the old separations for, and what makes them unnecessary?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá would have people attend each other’s places of worship and honour each other’s founders. What has been your experience of doing so, and what did Paine, who belonged to no church, miss or see?
Several talks set limits: the hostile, the harmful, the gossip. Jesus was called a friend of publicans and sinners. How do you tell prudence from avoidance?
One should be with people to give light or to receive it. Confucius says to have no friends not equal to oneself. What kind of company do you keep, and what kind do you avoid, and why?

outside.why: “A kindly tongue is the lodestone of the hearts of men.” Proverbs observed the same force working the other way on anger: a soft answer turneth away wrath.
Loving-kindness is to be shown “never asking whether they deserve to be loved”. Jesus gives the reason: God himself is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil.
“Human beings deserve respect, especially strangers.” Leviticus made it law: the stranger shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself.
Strangers especially. Exodus gives Israel a reason from memory: ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
“Contend not with anyone.” Paul, more guardedly: if it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
“Be kind to all strangers … make them feel at home.” Hebrews: be not forgetful to entertain strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
The friends are to be “as the rain of divine mercy which falleth upon every soil, as the rays of the sun” on garden and refuse heap alike. Both images are in the Sermon on the Mount.
“A pure tree is adapted to bestow a blessed fruit even upon those who throw stones at it.” Paul: if thine enemy hunger, feed him; overcome evil with good.
Peace will come “when every soul will have become the well-wisher of all mankind”. A line from a Roman comedy became the motto of that temper: nothing human is indifferent to me.

Bahá’u’lláh asks each soul to wish all mankind well. A doctor in Dostoevsky confesses that the more he loves humanity in general, the less he can stand any one person in particular. How is the general wish kept honest?
“He must not turn away his face from any soul.” Whitman: whoever walks a furlong without sympathy walks to his own funeral, dressed in his shroud.
The friends are to be “water to every thirsty one, a heavenly table to every hungry one”, healing to the sick. Jesus’ list is the same, and he counts each act as done to him.
“Be infinitely kind to the people and neighboring farms.” The Qur’an names both kinds of neighbour: the one who is of kin and the one who is not.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks farmers to be infinitely kind to the farms next door. Frost’s neighbour, mending the wall between two farms, says good fences make good neighbours. Is there a kindness in keeping a boundary?
In every city the friends should welcome a traveller “and show the utmost respect and consideration”. Abraham ran from his tent door to three strangers and had bread and a calf made ready.

Friends and relatives are to be treated with the utmost kindness, and “even … strangers”. Paul orders the same two circles the other way round: good unto all men, especially the household of faith. Does it matter which circle comes first?
“Call none a stranger … Be ye as if all men were your close kin.” Mozi taught it in China four centuries before Christ: regard another’s family as one’s own.

All men are to be treated as close kin. Mencius answered Mozi that to love all equally is to acknowledge no father. Can a love that makes no distinctions still honour the particular ties a person has?
“Some are ignorant; they must be trained … We must not detest him who is ailing.” Marcus Aurelius: men exist for the sake of one another; teach them then, or bear with them.
The one who is sick is to be cared for, not shunned. Jesus, asked why he ate with sinners: they that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.
One must deal “with all human beings of whatever religion or group” with friendship and trust. Peter, in a Roman officer’s house: in every nation he that feareth God is accepted with him.
“Should they show their enmity be friendly towards them.” The Qur’an: repel the evil deed with one which is better, and he who was an enemy will be as a bosom friend.
Fidelity for the unfaithful, justice for the unjust. The Tao Te Ching: to those who are not good to me, I am also good.

Earlier commandments of love, says ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, were kept within “the community of those in mutual agreement”. Jesus had pressed on the same limit: if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others?

Here is one of the limited commandments the tablet has in mind: Ezra telling a returned people to separate themselves from the people of the land. What was such a rule protecting, and what has changed that it can be lifted?
“Consort with all religions with amity and concord.” The Qur’an on speaking with Jews and Christians: argue not unless in a way that is better, and say, our God and your God is One.
“It is permitted that the peoples and kindreds of the world associate with one another.” Peter needed a vision to say the same: God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.
The glad tidings is a permission, which shows what it replaced. The woman at the well is surprised to be spoken to at all: the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans.

Consorting with all religions promotes “unity and concord”, and so order. Madison found the security of religious rights in the multiplicity of sects, each checking the others. Is peace between religions better served by friendship or by balance?
“Consort with the followers of all religions in a spirit of friendliness.” An Indian emperor had it cut in rock in the third century before Christ: whoever condemns other religions harms his own.
“Deal with all peoples and religions with utmost kindness.” The tenth Sikh Guru: the temple and the mosque are the same; all men are the same.
“We love their books, we read their scriptures, and we honor … the founders of their religions.” Gandhi asked for the same: mutual respect among the devotees of different religions.
To speak to each “from their own standpoint”. Ibn ‘Arabí’s poem: my heart has become capable of every form, a convent for monks, a temple for idols, the pilgrim’s Ka‘ba.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá would honour every scripture. Paine reached his own peace with the religions by believing none of their creeds: my own mind is my own church. Is respect for all religions easier from inside one of them or from outside them all?

People should go to each other’s churches and mosques, “for, in all of these worshiping places, the name of God is mentioned”. The Qur’an defends cloisters, churches, oratories and mosques in one breath, for that reason.
When people “mention each other’s leaders with due reverence”, contention will cease. Jesus stopped his disciples from forbidding an outsider: he that is not against us is on our part.
“Let there be no displeasing statement … concerning religions.” The Qur’an: revile not those unto whom they pray beside God, lest they wrongfully revile God.
“Do not pronounce as infidels those who have recognized God.” The Qur’an: say not unto one who offereth you peace, Thou art not a believer.
“Beware lest ye make God’s Word an occasion for your disputation.” Pope: for modes of faith let graceless zealots fight; his can’t be wrong whose life is in the right.
The one perfect love “can only be achieved by the power of the Divine Spirit”. Paul’s chapter on charity says what everything else is worth without it: sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.

“It is not possible for us to love everybody with a personal love, but we must love all humanity alike.” Aristotle agrees with the first half: one cannot be a friend to many in the perfect sense. What is the love that remains possible towards everyone?
“Even if they kill us, we must die with love for them.” Jesus: love your enemies, and pray for them which persecute you.
“It is easy for us to love a friend … but how difficult to love one who is without attraction.” Jesus: if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye?

If the love of God shines in the heart, it is seen reflected in every person. John puts the test in reverse: he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?
“We must consider all people … to be good.” Mencius argued it against a rival: human nature tends to good as water tends to flow downwards.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá hoped every one would be good and asked that all be considered so. Burns: man’s inhumanity to man makes countless thousands mourn. Is thinking well of everyone a judgment about people, or a way of treating them?
“We are all the children of one Father.” Malachi asks it as a reproach: have we not all one father? why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother?
“Deal ye one with another with the utmost love and harmony.” The Psalm: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
“Ye are the fruits of one tree, and the leaves of one branch.” Sa‘dí’s lines, which Persians have by heart: the sons of Adam are limbs of each other.
The friends “should weave bonds of fellowship with others”. Emerson on how any such bond begins: the only way to have a friend is to be one.
Consort with all “that perchance they may perceive the sweet savors of the utterance”. Paul uses the same sense for what a life gives off: we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ.
“Consort with the peoples of the world with spirit and fragrance.” The second sentence of the Analects: is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters?
All must associate “with radiant faces and illumined hearts”. Shammai, remembered as the stern one, said: receive all men with a pleasant countenance.
Goodly character spreads its fragrance, and “this fragrance hath ever been … a guide”. Whitman: we do not convince by arguments; we convince by our presence.
Where the fragrance of the Beloved is found, “associate with them and show humility toward them”. Proverbs: he that walketh with wise men shall be wise.

One should be with those “from whom he can get light, or … to whom he can give light”. Confucius allows only the first: have no friends not equal to yourself. What would be lost if everyone followed his rule?
Company should be for giving or receiving light. Proverbs: iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.

Being with people without purpose “is spending his time for nothing”. Seneca goes further and advises avoiding crowds, from which he comes home worse. How does one mix with everyone and still choose company?

The friends of Baku were “throughout these years of war, at peace with all communities”. Jeremiah’s letter to exiles in Babylon: seek the peace of the city, for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
Compassionate to all, in wartime. Lincoln at the end of a civil war: with malice toward none, with charity for all.
“All must hold fast unto wisdom” and associate with the people of the world with joy. Jesus sent his disciples out with both: wise as serpents, harmless as doves.
The command to consort with all religions means those who “are not antagonistic”. The Qur’an draws the line in the same place: God forbiddeth you not kindness to those who warred not against you.
Not with a Covenant-breaker. The early church had its own such rule about one who brought a contrary doctrine: receive him not into your house.
Love all religions, but avoid a fellow-believer of bad conduct. Paul made the same distinction: he did not mean the people of this world, but one called a brother who is such.
One cannot “consort with repose and pleasure with a thief” or keep a serpent in one’s sleeve. Paul quotes a Greek proverb: evil communications corrupt good manners.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá sets a limit at those who do harm. Jesus was reproached for having too few limits: a friend of publicans and sinners. Where is the line between keeping out of harm’s way and keeping away from people who need company?
“Leave them alone … have nothing to do with them.” The first verse of the Psalter: blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly.
Do not mix with bad people. Nittai the Arbelite in the Mishnah: keep a distance from an evil neighbour, do not become attached to the wicked.
“Do not spoil your tongue with the mention of evil people.” Proverbs explains what company does: make no friendship with an angry man, lest thou learn his ways.

After the limits just read, this tablet asks for a friend “to all the peoples of the earth, without any exceptions whatever”. Ben Azzai: do not despise any man, for there is no man that has not his hour. Can one keep away from someone without despising them?
“Overlook the faults of one another for My name’s sake.” Jesus gives a reason closer to home: the beam in thine own eye.
The friends are to consort “in amity and concord”. Paul’s wardrobe for it: put on kindness, humbleness of mind, forbearing one another, and above all charity.
The ungodly wait for a pretext to mock; discord gives it. Tertullian records what outsiders said when there was none: see how they love one another.
“The harm of no deed has equalled … the harm of discord.” Jesus made the opposite the sign: by this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
“Assist and help one another.” The Preacher: two are better than one; for if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow.
May the friends be renowned “for their cooperation and mutual assistance among strangers and kin”. Kropotkin made mutual aid his answer to those who saw only competition in nature.
“Though you are in that land and we are in this realm … yet in spirit we are in one gathering.” Paul to a church he had never visited: absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit.
All mankind are to become “the inhabitants of one City”. Diogenes, asked where he came from, is said to have answered that he was a citizen of the world.
One Order, one City. Garrison printed it at the head of his anti-slavery paper: our country is the world, our countrymen are all mankind.

“Mingle with all people and unfurl the banner of the oneness in the world of humanity.” Kipling’s famous first line says the twain shall never meet, and his next lines say when they do. What does it take, in his ballad and in this tablet?

Blessed are those “detached from all else but God” who yet consort with all. Thoreau kept three chairs: one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society. How do detachment and company fit in one life?
Detachment here does not mean withdrawal. Milton: I cannot praise a fugitive and cloistered virtue that never sallies out.

“Blessed is he who loves the world simply for the sake of the face of his generous Lord.” John’s letter: love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. Are they speaking of the same world?
“Love is God’s light among His creation.” John: he that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.
“Now is the time to cheer and refresh the downcast.” Isaiah’s commission begins with the same word twice: comfort ye, comfort ye my people.
“With faces joyous and beaming with light, associate with your neighbor.” A lawyer asked Jesus who his neighbour was, and was told a story about a stranger on a road.
“Be most loving one to another.” The rule that most traditions have in some form, as the Sermon on the Mount gives it.

Love of the neighbour is usually taught by the golden rule. Shaw: do not do unto others as you would that they should do unto you; their tastes may not be the same. What does kindness to a real stranger require that the rule leaves out?
Always “fellowship and love with friend and stranger alike”. Aristotle: without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods.
“Become loving friends to all humanity and a joy to the hearts … of all the world.” Coleridge’s mariner carries the circle wider: he prayeth best, who loveth best all things both great and small.
“Bestow affection upon every person, and adorn every gathering.” Peter: love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá remembers three friends by name and promises faithfulness to them. Proverbs: a friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
“Be unto them a loyal counsellor and a loving companion.” Confucius on what follows: virtue is not left to stand alone; he who practises it will have neighbours.
“Be as lamps unto the darkened world.” Jesus: ye are the light of the world; a city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
“Consort with all the peoples of the world with utmost love. All conflict … [is] forbidden.” Hillel: be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving mankind.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá listens patiently to “a stream of profitless, unspiritual talk” from daily callers. The Qur’an describes such servants: when the foolish address them they answer, Peace.
We are commanded to associate with all. Marcus Aurelius prepared for his own callers each morning: the busybody, the ungrateful, and yet we are made for co-operation.
“What is the Bahá’í Faith?” “Trust in God. Be kind to thy fellowmen.” Micah was asked what the Lord requires and answered as briefly.
Faith answered with kindness. The Qur’an’s short chapter says who denies religion: he who repels the orphan and does not urge the feeding of the needy.
“When ye meet anyone, consort with them in a spirit of fragrance and joy.” James describes a meeting where a gold ring gets the good seat and the poor man the floor.

luke-if-ye-love-them-which-love-you.text: For if ye love them which love you, what thank have ye? for sinners also love those that love them. And if ye do good to them which do good to you, what thank have ye? for sinners also do even the same

acts-not-call-any-man-common.text: And he said unto them, Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean

romans-live-peaceably.text: If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men

corinthians-evil-communications.text: Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners

corinthians-not-to-company.text: I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators: Yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, or extortioners, or with idolaters; for then must ye needs go out of the world. But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolator, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat

john-epistle-receive-him-not.text: If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed: For he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds

matthew-eateth-with-publicans.text: And it came to pass, as Jesus sat at meat in the house, behold, many publicans and sinners came and sat down with him and his disciples. And when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto his disciples, Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners? But when Jesus heard that, he said unto them, They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick

psalm-counsel-of-the-ungodly.text: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful

proverbs-walketh-with-wise-men.text: He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed

proverbs-no-friendship-with-an-angry-man.text: Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go: Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul

psalm-dwell-together-in-unity.text: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity

exodus-heart-of-a-stranger.text: Also thou shalt not oppress a stranger: for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt

job-stranger-did-not-lodge.text: The stranger did not lodge in the street: but I opened my doors to the traveller

ephesians-be-ye-kind.text: Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you

colossians-put-on-kindness.text: Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering; Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye. And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness

galatians-good-unto-all-men.text: As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith

john-epistle-loveth-not-his-brother.text: If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen

john-jews-have-no-dealings.text: Then saith the woman of Samaria unto him, How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans

james-respect-of-persons.text: My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons. For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool: Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts

peter-be-courteous.text: Finally, be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous: Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing

proverbs-friend-loveth-at-all-times.text: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity

ezra-separate-yourselves.text: Now therefore make confession unto the Lord God of your fathers, and do his pleasure: and separate yourselves from the people of the land, and from the strange wives

matthew-salute-your-brethren-only.text: For if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same? And if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others? do not even the publicans so

luke-friend-of-publicans.text: The Son of man is come eating and drinking; and ye say, Behold a gluttonous man, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners

quran-argue-not-save-in-better-way.text: And argue not with the People of the Scripture unless it be in (a way) that is better, save with such of them as do wrong; and say: We believe in that which hath been revealed unto us and revealed unto you; our Allah and your Allah is One, and unto Him we surrender.

quran-say-not-thou-art-not-a-believer.text: O ye who believe! When ye go forth (to fight) in the way of Allah, be careful to discriminate, and say not unto one who offereth you peace: "Thou art not a believer," seeking the chance profits of this life (so that ye may despoil him). With Allah are plenteous spoils. Even thus (as he now is) were ye before; but Allah hath since then been gracious unto you. Therefore take care to discriminate. Allah is ever Informed of what ye do.

quran-let-not-a-folk-deride.text: O ye who believe! Let not a folk deride a folk who may be better than they (are), not let women (deride) women who may be better than they are; neither defame one another, nor insult one another by nicknames. Bad is the name of lewdness after faith. And whoso turneth not in repentance, such are evil-doers.

quran-answer-peace.text: The (faithful) slaves of the Beneficent are they who walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace;

quran-nearest-in-affection.text: Thou wilt find the most vehement of mankind in hostility to those who believe (to be) the Jews and the idolaters. And thou wilt find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe (to be) those who say: Lo! We are Christians. That is because there are among them priests and monks, and because they are not proud.

avot-loving-peace.text: Hillel used to say: be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving mankind and drawing them close to the Torah

avot-do-not-despise-any-man.text: He used to say: do not despise any man, and do not discriminate against anything, for there is no man that has not his hour, and there is no thing that has not its place
